The feed pages this block; the page size is the feed's, not a design decision made here. Page 2 is the same file with a different offset, and a listing's detail page is the same five blocks as Unit 150 with different data — that is how 326 rows stay at one template.

What an archive like this gets asked

The tag question first, because it decides whether this archive is any use to you at all.

Can I buy a tag from one of these listings?
No, and this page sells no tags at all. These are guided hunts — a date, a guide and, sometimes, a bed. A landowner tag is a different product with its own verified inventory, and it lives on the unit guides. Confusing the two is the mistake the live site makes by selling both from one page.
Why do 326 listings share one page?
Because the rows differ and the page does not. Each listing keeps its own detail page for its own record, and the archive is the block that lists them: one row, a state, a species, a season and a band. A per-listing template would be 326 files that all say the same thing.
What about the 156 listing categories in the old sitemap?
They become filtered views of this one page — by state, by species — rather than 156 taxonomy templates. Same route, same block, one query string. The 2026-11-06 URL measurement flagged them as a decision; collapsing them is the decision.
Why show rows with no record at all?
Because the categories are real and the records are not here yet. A row that printed "call for details" would be a promise the file cannot keep; a row that prints No record is the truth about this design file, and the same row fills in when the record lands. Nothing in this archive is guessed to look complete.

Ask a person.

Whoever picks up can open the listing record while you are on the line — including whether the outfitter handles your licence, which is one of the five fields the Unit 150 listing leaves open.
